newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh to open talk with IMF for support.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh to open talk with IMF for support.

text.p: Bangladesh said on Saturday it would soon open negotiations with the International Monetary Fund for a $600 million package of balance of payment support.

"We will soon start formal discussion with the Fund. It's not because we are facing any crisis. It's just for precaution so that we are never caught by surprises," Finance Minister S.M.A.S Kibria told a news conference.
Kibria said: "We must have preparations. That is a prudent monetary management."

"We will have to look at their (IMF's) terms. The government is in power for only three months," Kibria said on his return home after attending the recent meeting of the borad of governors of the World Bank and IMF.

Finance ministry officials said Bangladesh needed agreement with the IMF on the assistance as Bangladesh was planning for a further relaxation of its foreign exchange regime to attract foreign private capital.
The finance minister said the country was enjoying a stable foreign exchange reserve that currently stood at $2 billion. "I am expecting it to grow in coming months with a rise in exports," he said.

Kibria said he also expected the flow of remittances from expatriate Bangladeshis would not be affected much despite the impact of thousands of workers who recently lost their jobs in the United Arab Emirates.
Bangladesh receives around $1.0 billion through workers remittances annually besides foreign aid disbursement of roughly $1.7 billion.

Bangladesh received balance of payment support from the IMF twice earlier, but only after agreeing to a tough adjustment prescription. The last IMF package, totalling $430 million in soft loans, ended in 1993.
The finance minister said he had asked the World Bank and IMF management to refrain from imposing rigid conditionalities on recipient countries.
Kibria said the government was making special efforts to expedite aid utilisation. The country now has about $5.6 billion in unutilised foreign aid in the pipeline.
